extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of narratology and creative writers studying storyworlds and immersion
extracted.subtask_description: Analytical framework for assessing and designing fictional storyworlds using possible-worlds semantics, focused on immersion, modal structures of characters, tellability, and plot coherence as world-conflict. Useful for narratology study and for writers who want principled criteria for worldbuilding and plot dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textual Actual World (TAW)
rubrics_metrics.description: A narrative constructs a 'textual actual world' — what is asserted to be true in the story. Around it cluster characters' belief-worlds, wish-worlds, obligation-worlds, fantasy-worlds, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how clearly the TAW is established and maintained, what propositions it asserts, and how it functions as the anchor for other private worlds; assess whether discrepancies between TAW and character worlds are intelligible and narratively productive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modal Structure of a Storyworld (K/W/O/I and fantasy worlds)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each character has private worlds: Knowledge world (K-world) — what the character believes is true; Wish world (W-world) — what the character wants to be true; Obligation world (O-world) — what the character believes ought to be true; Intention world (I-world) — what the character plans to do; Fantasy world — alternative imagined realities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the presence and articulation of these private-world types for characters, the distinctness and interaction of these modal layers, and whether the narrative leverages them to generate motivation, misunderstanding, and conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modal complexity of character private worlds
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree to which characters possess rich, differentiated private-world structures (beliefs, wishes, obligations, intentions, fantasies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use modal complexity as a metric of character depth: characters with multiple, conflicting private-worlds provide material for plot, tellability, and surprise. Evaluate examples where private-world richness produces nontrivial counterfactuals or unexpected actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot as world-conflict / Coherence of plot as movement among worlds
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot equals movement of the TAW relative to the private worlds of characters. The forward push comes from modal disequilibrium — gaps between what is, what is believed, what is wanted, and what ought to be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge plot coherence by how convincingly the narrative stages movements among worlds and resolves or escalates modal disequilibria; check that causal links among world-states are intelligible and that conflicts derive from believable discrepancies among worlds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of Minimal Departure / Strategic management of minimal departure
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers fill gaps in the storyworld by assuming it resembles the real world except where explicitly contradicted. The writer controls the minimal-departure budget — when to invoke worldhood, when to spend the suspension of disbelief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how the text signals departures from reality and whether those departures are justified, consistent, and economically used; assess whether the narrative over- or under-spends the reader's willingness to accept divergences from the real world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strength of immersion (spatial, temporal, emotional)
rubrics_metrics.description: Immersion has three distinct forms: spatial immersion — sense of being in a place; temporal immersion — being caught in the unfolding of time (suspense); emotional immersion — caring about characters and their fates. A great narrative produces all three.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rate the narrative's success at producing spatial presence, temporal engagement (suspense/flow), and emotional investment; consider trade-offs (e.g., techniques that enhance one form may reduce another) and cumulative immersive effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interactivity versus immersion
rubrics_metrics.description: For traditional fiction, interactivity (the reader's freedom to choose) is in tension with immersion (absorption). The novelist secures immersion by removing reader choice; interactive fiction must work harder to immerse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating interactive works, examine how choices are structured and whether they undermine or support spatial/temporal/emotional immersion; for non-interactive fiction, note how narrative closure and authorial control serve immersion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tellability
rubrics_metrics.description: A storyworld must be 'tellable' — worth narrating. Routine sequences fail. Tellability comes from modal complexity (rich private-world structures), counterfactual implications (what could have been), and surprising configurations of character worlds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the events and configurations in the story produce narratively interesting counterfactuals and surprises; determine if the material justifies narration (i.e., if it transcends routine experience through modal or configurational interest).

rubrics_metrics.name: Storyworld richness beyond the narrated events
rubrics_metrics.description: A storyworld is rich to the degree it sustains references beyond the narrated events, permits coherent inferences about unsaid matters, has internal logic that could generate further events, and awakens curiosity beyond the explicit text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate evidence of off-stage coherence: background facts, implied histories, causal potentials, and coherent systems of rules; richness scores higher when readers can plausibly infer unsaid facts and imagine further developments consistent with the world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluative criteria (summary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Summary list of narrative evaluation points: modal complexity of character private worlds; coherence of plot as movement among worlds; strength of spatial/temporal/emotional immersion; storyworld richness beyond explicit text; tellability; strategic management of minimal departure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this set as an integrated rubric: weight items relative to genre and medium (e.g., interactive vs. traditional fiction), and apply them to judge how effectively a narrative constructs and exploits its storyworld for meaning, suspense, and reader engagement.
